KEY MESSAGE 1...Dense river valley fog early this morning.

A combination of clearing skies, abundant low-level moisture in
part due to recent rain, and calm winds is resulting in areas of
fog this morning in the river valleys of western MD, eastern WV
and into the northern Shenandoah Valley in VA. Some of this fog
has become dense with visibility down to one quarter mile.

The Dense Fog Advisory has been expanded to include the 
northern Shenandoah Valley in VA, much of eastern WV, and into 
north-central MD given increasing visibility obs of 1/4 mile or 
less both on AWOS and traffic cams.

Fog will slowly burn off through mid morning. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Severe thunderstorms and some instances of 
flash flooding are possible on Sunday.

Overnight model guidance has come into a broad consensus
regarding the synoptic evolution for Sunday.

In the upper levels, a belt of seasonably strong westerlies 
will persist from the upper Great Lakes across the Saint 
Lawrence Valley into the Northeast and Canadian Maritimes. Broad
ascent on the equatorward side of this jet will persist much of
the time from early Sunday morning through late Sunday night.

Meanwhile, a pair of mid-level shortwaves, likely augmented by 
upstream convection over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, will track
across the Mid-Atlantic on Sunday. Although timing remains a 
bit uncertain, most guidance now agrees on an initial wave and 
attendant enhanced lift/flow during the morning. This initial 
wave may slow on its exit during the afternoon, only to be 
followed by another stout wave during the late afternoon and 
evening. W/NW flow in the 700-500 hPa layer increases to 30-40
kts, possibly higher depending on how these waves are deepened
by convection that occurs today/tonight upstream.

In the low levels, flow will also increase. This will allow a
sharp rise in theta-e, with PWs rising from around 1.75" at 09Z
to near 2.25" by 15Z. Further increases are progged into the
evening. Low-level/steering flow will lie parallel to a slowly
northward lifting warm front expected to bisect the area, so
despite the increased flow, backbuilding/repeating convection
seems plausible. Training plus the high PW airmass yields a
threat for excessive rain and flooding, perhaps mitigated a bit
by ongoing drought east of the Appalachians.

Areas that have seen recent heavy rain, or typical poor
drainage/urban areas would be rather susceptible to any such
excessive rainfall amounts. Of note, the 00Z HREF 3-hr PMM has
50-70% chance of exceeding 1" in the vicinity of western MD
early Sunday morning as a presumably weakening MCS treks into
the region. The probs for 3" are less than 10%, but recent heavy
rain in this area could raise at least a conditional flood
concern as early as the predawn hours on Sunday. Probs for 1"
and 3" in 3 hours are notably higher east of the Blue Ridge
during the afternoon hours. The latest HREF only goes out until
early Sunday evening, but guidance such as the NAM and extended
RAP suggest a further increase in PWs, low-level flow, and
SBCAPE Sunday night suggesting a lingering heavy rain threat.

In addition to any heavy rain threat is the potential for bands
of strong to severe thunderstorms. Increased flow down into the
low levels would be favorable for organized line segments
capable of mixing down damaging wind gusts in any organizing
cold pools. The saturated profiles could result in water loading
downdrafts, though the lack of mid-level dry air may keep DCAPE
low putting a ceiling on just how high damaging wind gusts can
get (most likely in the 50-65 mph range). The increased low-
level flow and SRH coupled with moist profiles could lend to the
threat of a few tornadoes as well.

Although the prospect of early morning clouds and precip may at
first glance seem to preclude a higher potential for heating and
severe weather later in the day, the high low-level moisture
content coupled with steady height falls aloft means that
heating will not need to be as robust to result in sufficient
CAPE for strong to severe convection, especially given the shear
that will be present.

Some severe weather or flood threat may persist into the night
given the above listed factors.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Seasonably warm conditions and daily shower and
thunderstorm chances are expected through Monday, before another
round of storms are possible on Thursday.

High pressure building across southern Quebec down into New
England will favor a mostly quiet day for the area today. An 
onshore component to the winds should favor a mix of clouds and 
sun through the day. Highs will rise into the mid/upper 80s with
any shower/thunderstorm chances confined to the Potomac 
Highlands across the central Shenandoah Valley toward I-64. 
Recent high-resolution models are showing an MCS racing across 
the Ohio Valley late today. Some of this could leak across the 
Alleghenies, but confidence remains low.
